<reason>PRO built a vivid, well-structured case (the "information tax" framing, APR/airfare analogies, a modest materiality-gated rule) and landed a clever rhetorical maneuver by casting CON's "recoup lost volume by raising commissions" as a confession that margins depend on customer ignorance. But CON's second rebuttal directly defused that dichotomy with a plausible, non-fake-precision mechanism: salience-driven loss-aversion causes order abandonment independent of whether the original price was fair, so lost volume doesn't require "ignorance" at all. PRO's closing never engaged this counter-mechanism, simply reasserting the "confession" framing rather than answering it — a real gap flagged explicitly (and fairly) by CON's closing. CON also pressed a live and only partially answered point: a rule blind to whether a gap is legitimate cost-recovery (packaging, dispatch, insurance) or markup effectively taxes honest and dishonest pricing alike, undermining PRO's "the customer decides" framing. CON's liability distinction (app-verified transaction prices vs. never-tested counter prices) was a sharper, more concrete workability point than PRO's rebuttal that "restaurants already type unaudited prices." PRO also incurred two format-clipped turns versus CON's one, a real execution cost. Overall CON did more of the decisive late-round work: neutralizing PRO's signature rhetorical weapon and keeping the harder economic and workability questions alive through closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B4.1–B4.2 (loss-aversion mechanism defusing PRO's "ignorance vs. genuine value" dichotomy), left unanswered in PRO's closing.</best_rebuttal>
